say.text: Before I teach anything, take a real exam stem. A guess is fine; it shows me where to start.
Which is the most common surgical emergency of the abdomen?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Acute appendicitis is the commonest surgical emergency of the abdomen, so the word 'most common' points straight at it.
You picked acute cholecystitis. It is tempting: it is a sharp, operative emergency, so it feels like the biggest one on the list.
But 'most common' counts how often a disease occurs, and appendicitis occurs more often [K1]. Frequency is the test here, not severity.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the qualifier next time: 'most common' asks for frequency, not severity [K1].

say.text: You picked perforated peptic ulcer. It is tempting: a perforation is dramatic and life-threatening, and exams love it.
But the stem asks for the commonest, and appendicitis is more frequent [K1]. Danger is a different question from frequency.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look at the qualifier again: 'most common' asks for frequency, and appendicitis leads [K91].

say.text: Reread the qualifier: 'most common' counts how many patients, not how sick they are. Which would fill the most places on an emergency surgical list?
So the answer is appendicitis, and the qualifier decides it. 'Most common' counts cases, and appendicitis tops that count among surgical emergencies [K1].
It is also the commonest non-obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy [K97]. Peak age is the second and third decades [K17], so think of it first in a young adult with pain.
Second problem, same rule: commit before I teach.
An 8-year-old has a recent viral illness and right iliac fossa pain. What is the commonest cause of the blockage in this child?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start with the age in the stem. Think about what fills a child's appendix, and what changes as the child grows up.
The answer is lymphoid hyperplasia, which often follows a viral illness and leads in children [K14][K94].
Faecolith is the adult cause, and you will meet it in a moment [K15].
Yes. In a child, lymphoid hyperplasia, often after a viral illness, is the usual cause of the blockage [K14][K94].
You picked faecolith. It is tempting: it is the classic blockage, and it is the cause most scans show.
But the age decides it. A child's appendix is full of lymphoid tissue, and hyperplasia of that tissue is the usual cause in children [K14][K94].

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the age before the cause: the stone is the adult pattern [K15][K95].

say.text: Worms are a real cause, so you are not far off.
But they are less common than lymphoid hyperplasia in a child [K16]. Pick the commonest cause, not any cause.
The mirror. Same rule, different age.
A 45-year-old's CT shows an appendicolith. What is the commonest cause of the blockage at this age?
Yes. In adults the usual cause is a faecolith, because the lymphoid tissue has shrunk by then [K15][K95][K23].
You picked lymphoid hyperplasia. It is tempting: it was the answer to the child stem a moment ago, so the cause feels familiar.
But the age has changed. Lymphoid tissue is richest in youth and atrophies with age [K23]. In adults the usual cause is a faecolith [K15][K95].

sure_note.text: You were sure, so notice the mirror: the same cause can be right at one age and wrong at another [K23].

say.text: The cause follows the age. Lymphoid tissue peaks in children and adolescents and then atrophies [K23], so lymphoid hyperplasia leads in the young [K14].
In adults a faecolith leads, and it carries a higher risk of perforation [K15][K95]. Worms and tumours are real but less common [K16].
